name: Sylvae
tagline: The right worker for the job, with a receipt.
description: A portable skill runner for human–agent teams: carry one SKILL.md instruction to a local model, a hosted API or an agent harness, choose the backend deliberately, and keep a durable run record another person can inspect.
status: Active development · v0.1.0 prototype runner with local review surface
motifCaption: The grove: shared knowledge, different workers, visible roots.

sv.title: Sylvae
sv.description: En portabel färdighetskörare: bär en SKILL.md-instruktion till en lokal modell, ett externt API eller en agent, välj körmiljö medvetet och behåll ett beständigt körningskvitto.

sections.title: Kunskap med rötter, inte leverantörslås
paragraphs: Sylvae kör en SKILL.md-instruktion mot Ollama, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode eller Anthropics API. Fyra av fem bakgrunder återanvänder CLI-verktyg du redan är inloggad på.
Välj nivå uttryckligen: billig, frontier eller agent. Automatik gissar aldrig att något är billigt. Explicita val spelar roll eftersom verkliga körningar kostar verklig tid, tokens och pengar.

sections.title: Börja i terminalen, fortsätt i granskningssidan
paragraphs: Installera från källkod, kör en liten färdighet mot en lokal modell och läs kvittot. En saknad bakgrund, en förbrukad budget eller ett nekat anrop är inte samma sak som ett misslyckat resultat.
De engelska fördjupningarna visar bakgrunder, granskningssidan och ombudsvägen för agenter. De blandar inte ihop lokal verifiering med ett beslut om driftsättning.

featuredPublication.label: The receipt problem / Brief 01
featuredPublication.imageAlt: A skill travels through an explicit tier choice to a backend; the run receipt returns to review while the audit chain stays separate.

highlights.label: 01 / Portability
highlights.title: The skill is not the vendor
highlights.text: Keep instructions in SKILL.md frontmatter and body. The same know-how travels between a local model, a hosted API and an agent harness without rewriting.

highlights.label: 02 / Honesty
highlights.title: A receipt, not a promise
highlights.text: Every run has an identity, a backend, a model, timing and an outcome. Unavailable budget, refused invocation and unsuccessful results are three different records.

highlights.label: 03 / Economy
highlights.title: Name the tier before spending
highlights.text: Cheap, frontier and agent are different resources with different fixed costs. Declared routing keeps a trivial prompt off a six-second agent bootstrap.

sections.title: Knowledge should grow roots, not vendor lock-in.
paragraphs: Sylvae loads a SKILL.md-format instruction and runs it through Ollama, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or the Anthropic API. Four of the five backends need no key of their own: they reuse command-line tools and accounts that are already configured.

Skills declare a tier in their frontmatter — cheap, frontier or agent — and the loader validates it. A misspelling is a clear error, not a silent fallthrough, because a typo that quietly routes to the most expensive backend is discovered on the bill.
A team can accumulate useful practices — summarising a change, checking a report, explaining disk use — as small reviewable instructions instead of habits locked inside one provider's harness.

sections.title: Routing is a promise about money and time.
paragraphs: Automatic routing reads the declared tier and nothing else. Cheap means a local model: free at the margin, unlimited, and yours to operate. Frontier means a capable hosted model on its own account. Agent means a real harness with tools, whose bootstrap overhead is fixed regardless of task size — several seconds and thousands of tokens before the work even starts.

A skill with no declared tier defaults to frontier. That is the safe choice, not the cheap one: automatic routing must never quietly spend an interactive budget or, worse, land a trivial prompt on an agent harness and look like it worked.

The documented measurements make the point concrete. The same trivial prompt cost roughly $0.171 and 28,000 tokens with default settings, and roughly $0.027 and 3,100 tokens after trimming unused setup. Those are observations from one experiment, not a savings guarantee — which is exactly why the choice stays explicit.

sections.title: Start at the terminal. Continue wherever suits the reviewer.
paragraphs: Install from source into a virtual environment and run one small skill against a backend you control. sylvae runs lists the evidence log with filters for skill, backend and status; sylvae show prints one run's input, output and error, or refuses an unknown or ambiguous identifier rather than guessing.

sylvae review opens a loopback-only page that browses the same records and can trigger new runs from a form — skill, backend, optional model, pasted input. Without a token it answers only to loopback hostnames, so a rebinding page cannot drive it; binding beyond loopback without a bearer token is refused. Triggered runs use real backends at real cost: there is no cheap preview mode.

An agent can delegate through the MCP server instead of doing the work inline. Two guards hold by default: delegation lands on the cheap local backend, and the subscription-sharing backend is refused over MCP because it would spend the caller's own interactive quota. Lifting either guard is an operator decision, never something a calling model grants itself.

sections.title: What exists, what was measured, what is still prototype.
paragraphs: Version 0.1.0 runs skills across five backends, keeps a JSONL evidence log, serves the local review page, projects WeftMark-compatible run identities, and wraps Nostoi audit commands with explicit unchecked states. The Phase-1 comparison ran two real skills across reachable backends and kept its raw records.

Known boundaries are documented rather than smoothed over. The local console entry point carries a stale pre-relocation path; shell completion, JSON output and piped rendering are covered separately. Bindings need their own builds and platform verification before being advertised as release targets.
The website is explanatory. Deploying this page does not expose the local review server, hand out a bearer token, or turn the prototype into a production service.

sections.title: Automatic decisions come after the gaps close.
paragraphs: The comparison report is explicit: automatic backend routing is worth building only after two gaps are fixed — ambiguous resolution outcomes that a router would have to decide between, and an interactive review flow that keeps a person in the decision. Until then, explicit routing is the contract, not a temporary inconvenience.

That ordering is deliberate. A router that retries a different backend on failure needs to distinguish a failure worth retrying from one that must stand, and needs somewhere to surface the choice. Building the router first would automate exactly the judgment the evidence says is missing.

Smaller steps come first: keeping the documented measurements current, widening binding platform coverage with verification rather than claims, and preserving the refusal behaviors — unknown identifiers, ambiguous prefixes, recursion-risk backends — that make the current tool trustworthy.

sections.title: A cooperative tool, not a replacement for responsibility.
paragraphs: Explicit routing, accessible run records and portable instructions are practical ways to support mutual cooperation: experiment without blind trust, spend deliberately, and keep the record where a colleague can find it.

Concerns about misuse, unpredictable behaviour or harmful uses of AI deserve serious attention. Sylvae records execution and helps organise bounded work; it does not itself guarantee that an agent is harmless or that a generated result is true. In Rebekah the runner sits inside a reproducible authenticated runtime, where human review and explicitly enabled governance add different kinds of oversight.

workflow.title: Write one useful skill
workflow.text: Describe the job and expected output in SKILL.md with a declared tier. Start small enough that another person can assess the result.

workflow.title: Choose a backend deliberately
workflow.text: Name a local model for a first experiment, or map tiers to your actual host and accounts. Read what auto would choose before letting it choose.

workflow.title: Read the receipt
workflow.text: Inspect input, output, model, timing and status. Unavailable, failed and successful runs answer different questions.

workflow.title: Bring the result into review
workflow.text: Correlate the run ID with WeftMark evidence, check audit integrity with Nostoi where useful, and keep the human judgment explicit.
workflow.linkLabel: Bring the threads to the loom

quickstart.title: Run one local skill
quickstart.summary: Use a source checkout, Python environment and an already configured Ollama installation. Download the model you intend to use and prepare a small input file.
quickstart.note: Model downloads need storage and bandwidth. Hosted and agent backends have their own credentials and costs; do not assume automatic routing is free.

commands.label: Install
commands.code:
git clone https://github.com/tabenius/sylvae.git
cd sylvae
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
pip install .

commands.label: Choose a model and run a skill
commands.code:
ollama pull mistral:latest
sylvae run skills/summarize-diff --backend ollama \
  --model mistral:latest --input /path/to/a/diff.txt

demonstration.label: The routing desk / Illustrated cases
demonstration.title: The same prompt can cost four different things.
demonstration.description: Select a case to see how a declared tier, an explicit backend and a recorded outcome relate. Backend and model names are the documented ones, not live measurements.
demonstration.disclaimer: Presentation-only illustrations. No model runs, no spending occurs, and no review is authorised by this explorer.

cases.title: Declared cheap stays local
cases.description: The skill names its tier; the router honours it without interpretation.
cases.conclusion: Illustration: explicit cheap work never leaves the machine. Operating the model remains your own cost to weigh.

cases.title: Undeclared defaults to frontier, not to cheap
cases.description: No tier key means the safe choice, on a separate account.
cases.conclusion: Illustration: the default protects an interactive budget from silent consumption; it does not promise the cheapest adequate answer.

cases.title: Agent work pays its bootstrap
cases.description: A harness with tools is a different resource from a bigger model.

fields.label: Fixed overhead
fields.value: Seconds and thousands of tokens, every run

cases.conclusion: Illustration: route multi-step work here deliberately; keep trivial prompts away from it.

cases.title: A missing budget is unavailable, not failed
cases.description: The run never happened, so there is nothing to debug in the skill.

fields.label: Next action
fields.value: Wait, re-authenticate, or choose another backend

cases.conclusion: Illustration: record the absence and act on it. Do not rewrite the skill to fix a run that never ran.

pages.title: From a skill to a useful receipt
pages.description: A practical path from an explicit backend choice to a run record and commit-bound evidence.

sections.title: Start small and explicit
paragraphs: Pick a skill and a small input whose quality you can assess. Name the backend and model rather than relying on someone else's host defaults.
Read the recorded outcome. A missing backend, unavailable budget or denied invocation is not the same as a skill that ran and produced an unsuccessful result.

sections.title: Make correlation deliberate
paragraphs: A coordinator can preallocate Sylvae's canonical 32-character lowercase run ID and use sylvae:run/<id> as WeftMark's evidence producer. Execute the real skill command through WeftMark when you need commit-bound evidence.
Keep the run receipt, engineering evidence and audit chain distinct. They complement each other; none can silently grant approval on behalf of a person.

sections.title: Finish with a human question
paragraphs: Does the result serve the purpose? What was not checked? Who can continue the work? Those questions connect the economical runner to a considerate, accountable workflow.

pages.title: Five backends, three tiers, one explicit choice
pages.description: What each backend reuses, what it spends, and why automatic routing refuses to guess.

sections.title: Local first, where it suffices.
paragraphs: Ollama runs a pulled model on your own machine through an explicit backend and model name. There is no API key and no per-call fee; the costs are hardware, electricity, maintenance and your attention to whether a small model's output is good enough.
A bare model name is prefixed to the litellm ollama/ convention when omitted. Pull the model before the run; a missing model is an unavailable run with a clear next action, not a mysterious failure.

sections.title: Hosted APIs spend someone's budget.
paragraphs: The Anthropic backend uses a configured API key; the claudecode backend reuses an existing Claude subscription through the local CLI with settings trimmed to shed unused bootstrap. Both are real metered inference with real latency.

The documented trimming experiment matters here: identical prompts differed by an order of magnitude in tokens and cost depending on setup. Defaults are not neutral, and Sylvae's flags exist to make the expensive parts visible rather than to promise they are gone.

sections.title: Agent harnesses are a tier of their own.
paragraphs: Shellout and opencode invoke real agent CLIs with their own authentication, tools and bootstrap overhead. They suit multi-step work and punish trivial prompts with fixed costs. Neither participates in cheap routing, and neither is selected by auto.

The claudecode backend shares an interactive quota, so a run spends the same allowance used for ordinary work. Hitting that limit is reported as unavailable. That distinction protects both the evidence log and the operator's afternoon.

sections.title: Auto reads the label; it does not read your mind.
paragraphs: With --backend auto, a declared cheap tier routes locally and a declared agent tier routes to a harness; anything undeclared, including a misspelling caught at load time, resolves to frontier. Per-tier overrides exist because the right target genuinely differs per operator.

Over MCP the guards tighten further: delegation defaults to cheap, the subscription-sharing backend is refused, and auto is refused outright, since tier routing could otherwise select a recursion-risk backend. An operator lifts these with flags; a calling model cannot grant them to itself.

pages.title: Three ways to meet a run: terminal, page, delegation
pages.description: The same evidence log, met through the CLI, a loopback page, or an agent handoff — each with its own authority.

sections.title: The terminal is the source of truth.
paragraphs: sylvae runs filters the log by skill, backend and status; sylvae show prints one run's metadata, input, output and error, refusing unknown or ambiguous identifiers. JSON output stays byte-clean under pipes, NO_COLOR or TERM=dumb, so scripts and humans read the same bytes.
Shell completion derives from the live command list. Nothing here needs a server, a token or a browser.

sections.title: The page is a convenience with a perimeter.
paragraphs: sylvae review serves the same records at loopback, with filtering, full-run expansion and a form that triggers real runs at real cost. Without a token it answers only to loopback hostnames; binding beyond loopback without a bearer token is refused.

Treat the page as a window onto the log, not a second authority. Triggered runs land in the same evidence log as CLI runs, and a page refresh never signs anything. Audit wrappers stay terminal commands by design.

sections.title: Delegation keeps the receipt.
paragraphs: Through MCP, an agent lists skills and runs one mid-task instead of doing the work inline — typically to spend a cheaper model rather than its own inference. Results return the run ID and namespaced runtime reference for correlation.

The recursion guards are the point: cheap by default, the subscription-sharing backend refused, auto refused. A coordinator may still preallocate a canonical run ID so the delegated run and external evidence share one identity. The receipt, not the transcript, is what travels onward.

sections.title: The audit trail is a separate record.
paragraphs: Nostoi wrappers verify the compatible ledger, attest a head with an explicit principal and key, and check attestations against pinned fingerprints. Daily run records and the audit chain are distinct; the browser excludes the chain from run lists.

Sidecar existence is not verified signing, and a signature never proves a test passed. The human step — signing, reviewing, approving — is never performed by a page load or a background agent. That separation is what makes the remaining evidence trustworthy.
